Course Description
The practical application of statistical thinking to contemporary issues; collection and organization of data; probability distributions; statistical inference; estimation; and hypothesis testing.
ACE 3 Outcomes: Use mathematical, computational, statistical, or formal reasoning (including reasoning based on principles of logic) to solve problems, draw inferences, and determine reasonableness. The reinforced skills for STAT 218 are Writing and Critical Thinking. STAT 218 will provide the student opportunities to achieve this learning outcome through readings, quizzes, and in-class activities. These assignments (together with exams) will be used by the instructor to assess achievement of the outcome. The final exam will be used by the Department of Statistics to carry out an overall assessment of STAT 218, and the course’s effectiveness at assisting students in achieving Outcome 3.

A common method of looking at quantitative data is with a boxplot. There are 6 components that make up the boxplot.

Minimum - the smallest value
Lower quartile (Q1) - value for which 25% of the data lie below (“median” of minimum and median
Median - the middle value (if there is an even number of values, then take the average of the two values in the middle)
Upper Quartile (Q3) - the value for which 75% of the data lie below (“median” of median and max)
Maximum - the largest value
Outliers - unusual extreme values in the data

This will be resistant to outliers

Suppose you collected the following ten values from your sample:
23 22 27 23 28 26 27 27 25 21
The first step is to arrange the numbers in order from least to greatest:
21 22 23 23 25 26 27 27 27 28

Since there is an even count of values, we need to take the average of the two values in the middle. Here, the values are 25 and 26, so the median is 25.5.
Note: There appears to be a discrepancy in the calculations of Q1 and Q3. I have seen some software include the use of the median and other software exclude the median. However, this discrepancy is negligible because the goal of quartiles for summarizing data is to get an idea of how the data behaves. In this class, you are not expected to calculate quartiles other than the median.

Boxplot on the data
21 22 23 23 25 26 27 27 27 28
Boxplot to scale

Here, you can see that Q1 is 23 and Q3 is 27. Therefore, the interquartile range is \(27 - 23 = 4\)
To find outliers, check values that are \(Q1 - 1.5 \cdot IQR\) or \(Q3 + 1.5 \cdot IQR\). Some software programs use points on the plot to specify values that are outliers.

title: Association and Confounding
text:
Observational Studies
The groups that you wish to compare are “just there.” Data is observed and collected on subjects without intervention of the results.
Examples: customer review surveys, teacher evaluations, smokers vs nonsmokers and lung cancer, etc.

title: Association and Confounding
text:
Experiments
You create the groups by what you choose to do to the people or the experimental units by assigning the conditions (i.e., _____________________ of groups)
Examples:

Assigning two diets to two different groups, then measuring the weight loss on each group
Assigning students to listen to either classical music or country music before an exam, then comparing the group scores

title: Association and Confounding
text:
Randomized Experiments
Experiments can be designed in such a way that we can balance out confounding variables. This is done through random assignment into different treatment groups. For randomized experiments, this means that each subject/participant is randomly placed into a group.
When conducting an experiment, our observational units are now called experimental units. Technical note: an experimental unit, by definition, is the smallest entity to which randomization can occur.

title: Association and Confounding
text:
Random Sampling vs. Random Assignment
Random Sampling: representative sample from population so we can extend conclusion to the larger population.

When random sampling is present, we can generalize the results to the population of interest.
When random sampling is not present, we cannot generalize results to the population of interest.

Example: Suppose that a study wants to estimate the average weight of the Western Meadowlark (state bird of Nebraska). Researchers get samples from random areas in the state of Nebraska.
Can we generalize the average weight to all Western Meadowlarks? To where can we generalize the results?

Random Assignment: produce similar groups so we can say that there is a cause-and-effect (causal) relationship between explanatory and response variables.

When random assignment is present, we can determine causation because the study “balances out” potential confounding variables.
When random assignment is not present, we cannot determine causation (only association). The confounding variables add bias into the results

Note: This is common with observational studies.

title: Final Project
text:
Description of Experiment
The purpose of your proposed experiment is to demonstrate your knowledge of the topics taught in our course. The following criteria must be met:

Experiment is feasible to conduct.
Outcomes occur due to a random (stochastic) process (no observational data).
Experimental units are able to be randomly assigned (if applicable).
Hypothesis is reasonable with respect to the subject matter.
Experiment can be ethically conducted.

title: Final Project
text:
Written Component
Due date: by the end of the scheduled final exam
The written component of the final includes writing up your experiment in the style of academic research. Your paper should be around 3-5 pages and include the following:

Introduction: describe what is currently known about your topic and your hypothesis/objective. If testing one group/process, what value is reasonable to test against? For two groups/processes, what difference provides practical significance? Include at least three sources and cite them correctly.
Methods: describe how you designed the experiment and the statistical test associated with the analysis. What are the experimental units, explanatory variable(s), response variable(s), and treatment groups? Describe how randomization occurs in the sampling and/or assignment. If appropriate, a diagram of your study would be helpful. What sample size is sufficient to meet the assumptions of the test?
Discussion: describe how the results of the experiment would fit into the literature, as well as potential limitations (no study is perfect!).

title: Final Project
text:
Presentation
Dates: last week of classes
Each group will have 7-10 minutes to present their experiment. In addition to the Introduction, Methods, and Discussion (as described above), you are required to analyze simulated data of the experiment and interpret it with correct conclusions using \(\alpha=0.05\). This includes calculating the appropriate point estimate, standardized statistic, and confidence interval. You may ask your instructor to help you obtain simulated data for your experiment (don’t wait until the week of presentations).

title: Chapter P
text:
Terminology
Data: the values measured or categories recorded on individual entities of interest
Population: the complete collection of ALL elements that are of interest for a given problem
Sample: a sub-collection of elements drawn from a population
Observation: the collection of measurements from a particular unit in a sample
Observational unit: the smallest unit to which data is collected
Variable: any measurable characteristic of an observation

title: Chapter P
text:
Gathering Evidence
Random Process: A random process is a process that can be repeated a very large number of times (theoretically infinitely many times) under identical conditions where outcomes cannot be known in advance.
Probability: The probability of an outcome is the long run proportion of times that outcome would occur if a random process were repeated a very large number of times under identical conditions.
Simulation: Artificially re-creating a random process.

Can be done using computer, dice, cards, coins, etc…

Simple Linear Regression (SLR) is a statistical method that allows us to summarize and study relationships between two continuous (quantitative) variables.
Examples: fuel efficiency of cars and their weights; grade point average and number of classes skipped for high school students
We will be using three methods to look at regression.

Scatterplots

title: Introduction
text:
Scatterplots
The first step is to analyze the data graphically through the use of scatterplots.

May have called them x − y plots
The explanatory/predictor variable goes on the x−axis
The response variable goes on the y−axis
There is a dot on the plot for each point in the data set

To visually analyze, will look at four aspects:

Direction: positive, negative or no relationship
Form: Is the association linear (do the points follow a linear pattern) or some more complicated curve?
Strength

How closely do the points follow a pattern?
If you imagine a line through the points, the points all fall pretty close to that line, the association is fairly strong

Unusual Observations

Are there any points that do not seem to adhere to the overall pattern

title: Introduction
text:
Example: Growing Plates?
Research question: Are dinner plates getting larger?
There are many recent articles and TV reports about the obesity problem. One reason some have given is that the size of differ plates are increasing. Are these black circles the same size, or is one larger than the other?



A picture containing shape Description automatically generated


The circle on the right is about 20% larger than the one on the left. This suggests that people will put more food on larger dinner plates without knowing. This is known as Delboeuf illusion.
Researchers gathered data to investigate the claim that dinner plates are growing by using American dinner plates sold on ebay on March 30th, 2010 (Van Ittersum and Wansink, 2011). The year manufactured and diameter are given below.



Table Description automatically generated


Both year (explanatory) and diameter (response) are quantitative. Each dot on the plot below represents one plate.



Chart, scatter chart Description automatically generated


The data is trending upward, which indicates a positive association. We also do not see any curves within the data, which suggests this is a linear trend.
The regression equation is \(\widehat{y} = a + bx\):

a is the y-intercept
b is the slope
x is a value of the explanatory variable
ŷ is the predicted value for the response variable

For a specific value of x, the corresponding distance \(y - \widehat{y}\) (or actual – predicted) is a residual

title: Introduction
text:
Residual
A residual is the vertical distance from a point to the regression line. This can also be described as the difference between an observed response and the corresponding predicted response.
Residual = Observed - Predicted

Negative residuals fall below the line (overestimate)
Positive residuals are above the line (underestimate)
Each observational unit has a residual

title: Introduction
section: Regression Line for Growing Plate example
text:
Regression Line for Growing Plate example
Software will calculate the coefficients for us. The least squares line for the dinner plate data is \(\widehat{y} = - 14.8 + 0.0128x\)
Or \(\widehat{diameter} = - 14.8 + 0.0128(year)\)

This allows us to predict plate diameter for a particular year.

What is the predicted diameter for a plate manufactured in 2000?
-14.8 + 0.0128(2000) = 10.8 in.
What is the predicted diameter for a plate manufactured in 2001?

-14.8 + 0.0128(2001) = 10.8128 in.

How does this compare to our prediction for the year 2000?

0.0128 larger

Slope b = 0.0128 means that diameters are predicted to increase by 0.0128 inches per year on average
Slope is the predicted change in the response variable for one-unit change in the explanatory variable. Both the slope and the correlation coefficient for this study were positive.

The slope is 0.0128
The correlation is 0.604

The slope and correlation coefficient will always have the same sign.
The y-intercept is where the regression line crosses the y-axis or the predicted response when the explanatory variable equals 0.

We had a y-intercept of -14.8 in the dinner plate equation. What does this tell us about our dinner plate example?

Dinner plates in year 0 were -14.8 inches.




How can it be negative?

The equation works well within the range of values given for the explanatory variable, but fails outside that range.

Our equation should only be used to predict the size of dinner plates from about 1950 to 2010.

title: Introduction
text:
Coefficient of Determination
While the intercept and slope have meaning in the context of year and diameter, remember that the correlation does not. It is just 0.604. However, the square of the correlation (coefficient of determination or r2) does have meaning.

r2 = 0.6042 = 0.365 or 36.5%
36.5% of the variation in plate size (or the response variable) can be explained by its linear association with the year (the explanatory variable).

For several years in the 1990s, Kristen Gilbert worked as a nurse in the intensive care unit (ICU) of the Veterans Administration Hospital in Northampton, Massachusetts. Over the course of her time there, other nurses came to suspect that she was killing patients by injecting them with the heart stimulant epinephrine. Gilbert was eventually arrested and charged with these murders. Part of the evidence presented against Gilbert at her murder trial was a statistical analysis of 1,641 eight-hour shifts during the time Gilbert worked in the ICU. For each of these shifts, researchers recorded two variables: whether or not Gilbert worked on the shift and whether or not at least one patient died during the shift.
Results: Of the 257 shifts that Gilbert worked, 40 of the shifts had a patient that died. Of the 1,384 shifts that Gilbert did not work, 34 had a patient that died

\({\widehat{\mathbf{p}}}_{\mathbf{NG}}\mathbf{=}\frac{Patients\ died\ Given\ Gilbert\ NOT\ Working}{Total\ Shifts\ Gilbert\ Does\ NOT\ Work} = \frac{34}{1384} = 0.025\)

“How many times as large the risk of an outcome is for one group compared to another”

From the example,

\[\frac{{\widehat{\mathbf{p}}}_{\mathbf{G}}}{{\widehat{\mathbf{p}}}_{\mathbf{NG}}}\mathbf{=}\frac{\frac{40}{257}}{\frac{34}{1384}} = \ \frac{0.15}{0.02} = 7.5\]
Interpretation: The proportion of deaths is 7.5 times as large on a Gilbert shift than a non-Gilbert shift.
In general, it is common to calculate the relative risk using the larger proportion in the numerator.
A word of caution, the use of relative risk can sometimes be misleading. Consider the following two examples:



\[\frac{0.0005}{0.0001} = 5\] \[\frac{0.5}{0.1} = 5\]

However, the study was observational and thus cannot conclude that Gilbert caused the deaths (no random assignment to shifts). One such possible alternative is that Gilbert possibly worked shifts where more patients die.

text:
Example: Swimming with Dolphins
Is swimming with dolphins therapeutic for patients with clinical depression? A 2005 study (Antonioli and Reveley) recruited 30 subjects with a clinical diagnosis of mild to moderate depression. These 30 subjects went to an island oﬀ the coast of Honduras, where they were randomly assigned to one of two treatment groups. Both groups engaged in one hour of swimming and snorkeling each day, but one group did so in the presence of bottlenose dolphins and the other group did not. However, note that participants in the dolphin group and the control group experienced identical conditions except for the presence of dolphins. At the end of two weeks, each subject’s level of depression was evaluated. The researchers looked to see whether or not the subject achieved substantial reduction (improvement) in their depression. They found that, of the 10 subjects in the dolphin group, 9 showed substantial improvement. Of the 20 in the control group, 3 showed substantial improvement.

text:
Standardized Statistic

General Formula:

\[SS = \frac{observed\ statistic\  - null\ value}{SD\ of\ the\ null\ (or\ SE)}\]

Two Group Categorical Specific:

\[SS = \frac{\left( {\widehat{p}}_{1}\  - \ {\widehat{p}}_{2} \right) - 0\ \text{~}}{SE} = \frac{\left( {\widehat{p}}_{1}\  - \ {\widehat{p}}_{2} \right) - 0\ \text{~}}{\sqrt{\overline{p}\left( 1 - \overline{p} \right)(\frac{1}{n_{1}} + \frac{1}{n_{2}}\ )}}\]

title: Section 5.1: Comparing Two Groups - Categorical Response
text:
Confidence Interval

General Formula:

\[\ Observed\ Statistic \pm Multiplier*SE\]
Margin of Error (MOE)
Recall that we had a different standard error formula in Chapter 1 when we are calculating for either a standardized statistic or confidence interval when the data is categorical. For confidence intervals,

\[SE = \sqrt{\frac{{\widehat{p}}_{1}(1 - {\widehat{p}}_{1})}{n_{1}} + \frac{{\widehat{p}}_{2}(1 - {\widehat{p}}_{2})}{n_{2}}}\]

Two Group Categorical Specific (95% Confidence):

\[\widehat{(p_{1}} - \widehat{p_{2}}\ ) \pm 2*\sqrt{\frac{{\widehat{p}}_{1}(1 - {\widehat{p}}_{1})}{n_{1}} + \frac{{\widehat{p}}_{2}(1 - {\widehat{p}}_{2})}{n_{2}}}\]
Interpretation

We are 95% confident that the long run difference in proportion of “context here” between group 1 and group 2 is between ________ and _________.

Alternately… Be careful with wording on this one!

We are 95% confident the true proportion of “context” in “group 1” is ”lower limit” to ”upper limit” ”more or less” than the true proportion of ”context” in”group 2.”
With differences, if 0 in interval, NOT significantly different

Recall from Chapter 6 that we were comparing two groups with a quantitative response. The steps to comparing two groups involved calculating the sample means, finding the difference, and then conducting a hypothesis test.

title: Chapter 7
text:
Paired Designs
Paired Designs: response variables come in pairs, with one response value in the pair belonging to each explanatory variable group.
Pairs can come from matching individuals OR measuring the same individual twice (repeated measures).
With the pairs, we can focus on the differences as our response. There are advantages to using a paired design. In many cases, it is better to measure the response on the same person/thing (because of similar units, measured over time, etc.). Pairing helps us to look at the differences between the explanatory variable groups rather than the differences between the observational units. If your design is a matched paired design, it must be analyzed as matched pairs.
